transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in today?

My sleep has been completely off for weeks—either I’m up most of the night with my mind going or I crash and still wake up feeling worn out. It's just getting really hard to keep up with everything when I'm this exhausted.
Have you also been feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest in things you usually enjoy, not just tired?

Yes, when my energy drops, it feels like this heavy gray cloud settles over me and I just feel completely useless and guilty. I've lost all interest in things I used to love, like knitting or helping at the food pantry, and now I just stare at my yarn or ignore texts from people.
Have these low mood and feelings of worthlessness been present most days, even before your sleep problems started, or do they seem to come after you’ve been sleep-deprived?

Honestly, they both started around the same time, about three months ago when all the family stress really hit. The heavy, useless feelings usually settle in when my energy drops and I crash after those wired, sleepless nights, so they've been going hand-in-hand this whole time.
Have you had any previous episodes of low mood or loss of interest that lasted two weeks or more, before this current three-month period?
No, I've never experienced anything like this before. I've always been a pretty steady person until all of this started about three months ago.

inference_history.note: Previously the candidates included F32 (depressive episode), F33 (recurrent depressive disorder), G47.0 (insomnia), and G47.1 (hypersomnia). Based on the conversation, the patient describes a concurrent onset of low mood, anhedonia, guilt, and sleep disturbances (insomnia with periods of exhaustion) approximately three months ago, linked to psychosocial stressors. The depressive symptoms and sleep issues appear to be interdependent rather than one clearly preceding the other. The absence of a prior distinct episode suggests this is a current major depressive episode rather than a recurrent course, making F33 less likely but still possible if future history reveals prior episodes. Insomnia (G47.0) and hypersomnia (G47.1) are present as symptoms but appear to be part of a broader mood disorder rather than primary sleep disorders, given the co-occurrence and mutual worsening with mood symptoms. Therefore, primary sleep disorders are now considered less likely as standalone diagnoses, leaving F32 and F33 as the primary differential. Further clarification on prior depressive episodes is needed to distinguish between them.
